questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

options.text: They are interchangeable terms for the same concept
Authentication verifies identity; authorization determines permissions
Authorization verifies identity; authentication determines permissions
Authentication is for users; authorization is for API services

questions.explanation: Authentication answers 'Who are you?' (verify identity via password, token, biometrics). Authorization answers 'What can you do?' (check permissions for resources/actions). Authentication must happen first—you can't authorize an unknown user. AWS IAM separates these: authentication via credentials, authorization via policies.

questions.question: What is a JWT (JSON Web Token)?

options.text: A database format for storing user credentials
A self-contained token containing claims, signed for integrity verification
A JavaScript framework for authentication
A network protocol for secure communication

questions.explanation: JWT is a compact, self-contained token with three parts: header (algorithm), payload (claims like user ID, roles, expiration), and signature (integrity verification). Stateless—server doesn't need session storage. Auth0, Firebase, and most modern APIs use JWTs. The signature prevents tampering; anyone can decode the payload but can't modify it without invalidating the signature.

questions.question: What is OAuth 2.0?

options.text: An encryption algorithm for securing passwords
An authorization framework for delegated access without sharing credentials
A database for storing authentication tokens
A programming language for security applications

questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 enables delegated authorization: users grant apps limited access to their resources on another service without sharing passwords. 'Login with Google' uses OAuth—the app gets an access token with specific scopes, not your Google password. GitHub, Twitter, and Facebook all provide OAuth. It's authorization, not authentication (OpenID Connect adds authentication on top).

questions.question: What is the difference between session-based and token-based authentication?

options.text: No functional difference, just implementation details
Session-based stores state on server; token-based is stateless with self-contained tokens
Token-based is inherently less secure than sessions
Session-based is only for mobile applications

questions.explanation: Session-based: server stores session data (user info, permissions), client holds session ID cookie. Token-based (JWT): token contains all info, server is stateless. Token-based scales better (no shared session store needed across servers) but tokens can't be easily revoked mid-flight. Netflix uses tokens for their distributed architecture; traditional web apps often use sessions.

questions.question: What is RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)?

options.text: A backup system for authentication data
Authorization model where permissions are assigned to roles, and users are assigned roles
A database type optimized for access control
An encryption method for role information

questions.explanation: RBAC: define roles (admin, editor, viewer), assign permissions to roles, assign roles to users. Simplifies management—change role permissions once, all users with that role are updated. AWS IAM, Kubernetes, and most enterprise systems use RBAC. Alternative: ABAC (Attribute-Based) for more dynamic, context-aware authorization.

questions.question: What is an access token vs refresh token?

options.text: They serve the same purpose with different names
Access token: short-lived, used for API calls. Refresh token: long-lived, used to get new access tokens
Refresh token is sent with every API call
Access tokens never expire by design

questions.explanation: Access token: short-lived (15 minutes to 1 hour), sent with each API request, acceptable if stolen briefly. Refresh token: long-lived (days/weeks), stored securely, used only to obtain new access tokens when the access token expires. This limits damage if access token is stolen while avoiding constant re-authentication. Spotify and Google use this pattern.

questions.question: What is Single Sign-On (SSO)?

options.text: Signing documents once electronically
Authentication allowing users to access multiple applications with one login
Using a single password for all accounts
Signing in once per calendar day

questions.explanation: SSO: authenticate once with an identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace), access multiple applications without re-authenticating. Improves UX (fewer logins to remember), security (centralized auth, easier to enforce MFA), and management (single point for access control and revocation). Enterprise standard for internal tools.

questions.question: What is the principle of least privilege?

options.text: Give everyone admin access for convenience
Grant only the minimum permissions necessary to perform a task
Remove all permissions by default
Privilege levels are not important for security

questions.explanation: Least privilege: users and services get only the permissions they need, nothing more. Limits blast radius if an account is compromised—an attacker with read-only access can't delete data. AWS IAM policies, Kubernetes RBAC, and database grants should all follow this principle. Regular access reviews revoke unnecessary permissions.

questions.question: True or False: JWTs can be revoked instantly like sessions.

options.text: True - JWTs support immediate revocation
False - JWTs are stateless and can't be easily revoked

questions.explanation: JWTs are stateless—the server doesn't track issued tokens, so it can't invalidate them. Workarounds: short expiration times (force refresh), token blocklists (adds state), or refresh token revocation (user must re-authenticate). Sessions can be invalidated instantly by deleting server-side session data. This is a key JWT tradeoff: scalability vs. revocation control.

questions.question: What is API key authentication?

options.text: Physical key for accessing server rooms
Simple authentication using a secret string passed with requests
Keyboard shortcuts for API access
Database primary keys for API records

questions.explanation: API key: a simple secret string identifying the caller, typically passed in headers (X-API-Key) or query parameters. Easy to implement but limited: no user context (identifies app, not user), hard to rotate without breaking clients, often logged accidentally. Better for service-to-service or public APIs with rate limiting than user authentication. Stripe and Twilio use API keys.

questions.question: What is MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication)?

options.text: Using multiple passwords for the same account
Authentication requiring multiple independent factors (something you know, have, are)
Logging in multiple times for verification
Having multiple user accounts for security

questions.explanation: MFA requires multiple independent factors: knowledge (password), possession (phone, hardware key like YubiKey), inherence (fingerprint, face). Compromising one factor isn't enough—attacker needs your password AND your phone. Google reports MFA blocks 99.9% of automated attacks. Essential for sensitive systems; increasingly required for compliance.

questions.question: What should happen when a JWT expires?

options.text: Continue using it until the server rejects it
Use refresh token to obtain new access token, or re-authenticate
Delete the user account automatically
Ignore expiration for better user experience

questions.explanation: Expired JWTs should be rejected immediately—the 'exp' claim exists for security. Client uses refresh token (if available and valid) to get a new access token without user interaction. If refresh token is also expired or revoked, user must re-authenticate. Never accept expired tokens; never extend expiration client-side. This is fundamental to token security.
